name: 5:2 diet / alternate-day fasting

lead: The 5:2 diet restricts intake to roughly 500 to 600 calories on two non-consecutive days and eats normally on the other five. Alternate-day fasting alternates very low-calorie days with normal days. People use both to build a weekly calorie deficit and lower body fat for a leaner look.

The low days cut weekly intake, so fat and some lean mass are lost. Reviews report weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent in most human studies, comparable to continuous calorie restriction, and reviews suggest exercise to help retain lean mass.

paras: Followers pick two fast days a week (5:2) or fast every other day, eating normally in between. Many pair it with resistance training to keep muscle. Results build over weeks as the weekly deficit accumulates.

Hunger, irritability, dizziness and headaches are common early on. Health bodies say it is not recommended for pregnancy, children, adolescents, older adults, underweight people or those with eating disorders.

angle.text: Very low-calorie fast days create a weekly calorie deficit that lowers body fat and gives a leaner look. Trials show weight loss comparable to ordinary dieting, and appearance outcomes themselves have not been studied.

lead: The 5:2 diet and alternate-day fasting are two forms of intermittent energy restriction used to get leaner. The 5:2 pattern has two non-consecutive low-calorie days of roughly 500 to 600 calories and normal eating on the other five; alternate-day fasting alternates a very low-calorie day (under about 25 percent of usual needs) with a normal "feast" day, and a modified version allows up to 25 percent of calories on fast days [1]. The appearance payoff people seek is lower body fat: a slimmer waist, more visible muscle definition and a sharper face.

The 5:2 pattern was documented in a 2011 article by Harvie and colleagues and was popularized in the UK and Australia by Michael Mosley through the 2012 BBC Horizon documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer; his 2013 book The Fast Diet, written with Mimi Spencer, followed [1][2]. Reviews report weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent in most human studies, and a 2023 meta-analysis of 24 trials concluded that intermittent fasting produced weight loss comparable to continuous calorie restriction, ranking alternate-day fasting highest of the three regimens compared [1][3].

Both patterns are grouped with time-restricted eating under intermittent fasting, an umbrella for diets that alternate periods of fasting with ad libitum eating [4]. Intermittent fasting was named the most popular diet in the US in a 2018 survey by the International Food Information Council, according to Wikipedia [1]. Its reviewers describe it chiefly as a weight-management and cardiometabolic strategy; the appearance gain for people who use it comes from lower body fat.

On looksmaxxing forums the approach is described as a way to cut without counting calories every day. One looksmax.org thread titled '5/2 fasting is the best way to get shredded' has a user reporting a drop from 340 to 271 lbs in two months [5].

paras: Both protocols are grouped with time-restricted eating under intermittent fasting, all involving alternating periods of fasting and ad libitum eating [4]. Periodic or whole-day fasting with water only is a separate category [1]. Wikipedia lists four main methods: time-restricted eating (often an 8 to 12 hour daily window), alternate-day fasting, the 5:2 diet and periodic fasting of more than 24 hours [1].

The appeal described for the 5:2 and alternate-day formats is that dieting is concentrated into specific days, so that other days are eaten normally. Researchers note that adherence to daily energy restriction tends to decline over time, which is one of the reasons intermittent regimens were developed [6].

In the 5:2 diet, two non-consecutive days each week are limited to roughly 500 to 600 calories, about a quarter of usual intake, with normal eating on the other five days [1]. Alternate-day fasting alternates a 24-hour fast day with a 24-hour non-fasting day; the complete version has no calories on fast days, while modified alternate-day fasting allows up to 25 percent of calorie needs on fast days [1]. Time-restricted eating, the third common form, confines eating to a daily window such as 6 hours, which gives 18 hours of fasting [7].

In the original Harvie trial in young overweight women, the intermittent arm ate about 2,710 kJ on two days a week, while the comparison arm ate about 6,276 kJ every day, so that both arms had a 25 percent weekly energy restriction [8]. The original 5:2 trials focused on calorie content rather than a specific food pattern [2]. In a 2024 Diabetes Care trial, 5:2 days were delivered with a formula diet rather than ordinary food [9].

Reviewers describe the mechanism in two parts. Calorie intake falls by about 10 to 30 percent from baseline across all of these regimens, and the regimens intermittently shift metabolism toward fatty acids and ketones [7][10].

Therapeutic fasting for obesity has been studied since 1915, with renewed medical interest in the 1960s after an enthusiastic report by Bloom and colleagues; those early fasts lasted from 1 to 14 days, and the enthusiasm reached lay magazines, which prompted researchers and clinicians to caution against unmonitored fasting [1].

The 5:2 approach was first documented in a 2011 paper co-authored by Michelle Harvie, Mark Mattson and 14 other scientists [1]. The accompanying randomized trial, published in the International Journal of Obesity, allocated 107 overweight or obese premenopausal women to a 25 percent energy restriction delivered either on two days a week or continuously for six months [8]. Both groups lost similar weight (6.4 kg intermittent, 5.6 kg continuous), with comparable changes in leptin, CRP, cholesterol and blood pressure, and modestly larger falls in fasting insulin with the intermittent approach [8].

Michael Mosley (1957 to 2024) was a British journalist and presenter who worked for the BBC from 1985 and had presented on camera since 2007 [2]. On 6 August 2012 his Horizon episode Eat, Fast and Live Longer on BBC Two popularized the 5:2 diet in the UK and Australia; he said he learned of the approach from the neuroscientist Mark Mattson, and his BBC Health article followed in the same month [1][2].

The Fast Diet, co-written with Mimi Spencer, was published by Short Books in early 2013 [2]. Mosley later promoted the Fast 800, an 800-calorie-a-day plan, and The Fast 800 Keto in 2021, and wrote The 8-Week Blood Sugar Diet in 2016 [2]. He died on 5 June 2024 while on holiday on the Greek island of Symi; an inquest in December 2024 recorded the cause as unascertainable, most likely heat stroke or an unidentified pathological cause [2].
Intermittent fasting more broadly was named the most popular diet in the US in a 2018 survey by the International Food Information Council, according to Wikipedia [1].

People using these protocols for appearance typically aim to lose fat while keeping training volume. Like other diets, intermittent fasting typically induces loss of both fat and lean mass, and a 2025 narrative review proposes exercise as an adjunct to retain lean mass [4]. A 2024 randomized trial in adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes compared a 5:2 diet (two days per week of formula-diet energy restriction) with a high-intensity interval plus resistance exercise program and routine education on glycemic control and cardiometabolic health [9].

Wikipedia reports that fasting does not appear to benefit athletic performance [1]. Fasts of several days, a separate practice from 5:2, are described as losing about two-thirds of early weight as lean tissue rather than fat [11].

A 2025 BMJ systematic review and network meta-analysis of 99 randomized trials with 6,582 adults compared intermittent fasting (alternate-day, time-restricted and whole-day fasting), continuous energy restriction and ad libitum diets on body weight and cardiometabolic outcomes [12]. A 2020 systematic review in Canadian Family Physician covered 27 trials and found weight loss of 0.8 to 13.0 percent of baseline weight with no serious adverse events, with 12 studies comparing intermittent fasting with calorie restriction reporting equivalent results [13].

A 2023 meta-analysis of 24 trials (1,768 participants) found that intermittent fasting produced weight loss similar to continuous restriction (mean difference 0.26 kg), with compliance above 80 percent in trials shorter than 3 months [3]. A 2024 umbrella review reported improvements in waist circumference, fat mass, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting insulin, with a smaller blood-pressure benefit than continuous calorie restriction [1]. A 2021 review reported that moderate alternate-day fasting for 2 to 6 months reduced weight, BMI and cardiometabolic risk factors [1]. A Cochrane review found it uncertain whether intermittent fasting prevents cardiovascular disease [1].

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 randomized trials of the 5:2 diet in people with overweight or obesity (1,393 participants) reported significant reductions versus controls in body weight, BMI, waist circumference, body fat percentage, fat mass, fat-free mass, LDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure and insulin resistance, with no difference in visceral fat, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol or fasting glucose [8]. The authors reported no serious adverse events in the 5:2 groups, only mild physical and psychological effects on fasting days that resolved on their own [8].
The Harvie randomized trial found six-month weight loss similar to continuous restriction [8]. A 2024 trial in adults with type 2 diabetes compared 5:2 dieting with an exercise program [9].

The 2017 JAMA Internal Medicine trial randomized 100 obese adults (86 women, mean BMI about 34) to alternate-day fasting, daily calorie restriction or no intervention for a year, with a 6-month weight-loss phase and a 6-month maintenance phase [14]. Weight loss was similar in the two diet groups, dropout was 38 percent for alternate-day fasting versus 29 percent for calorie restriction and 26 percent for controls, and LDL cholesterol was higher in the fasting group at 12 months; the authors concluded alternate-day fasting was not superior to daily restriction [14].

A 2025 BMC Medicine randomized trial in adults with obesity compared a ketogenic diet, time-restricted eating and alternate-day fasting on weight loss [15]. A 2022 randomized trial in the Journal of Nursing Research looked at intermittent fasting for weight loss and cardiometabolic risk reduction [16]. A 2023 randomized trial examined alternate-day fasting combined with aerobic exercise in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease [17].

A 2024 network meta-analysis of 47 trials (3,363 participants) ranked alternate-day fasting first for weight loss (mean difference minus 3.42 kg), ahead of time-restricted eating (minus 2.25), short-term fasting and continuous restriction (minus 1.59); weight regain appeared in many analyses by 4 to 6 months, and short-term fasting was associated with lean mass decline [8]. A 2022 meta-analysis of 16 trials (1,438 participants) of at least 12 weeks found no significant difference between intermittent and continuous restriction in weight, waist or body fat, with attrition of 26.6 percent versus 24.1 percent, concluding it was comparable but not superior [8].

Reviews of cardiometabolic outcomes report that alternate-day fasting, the 5:2 diet and time-restricted eating produced mild to moderate weight loss of 1 to 8 percent from baseline and reductions in blood pressure, insulin resistance and oxidative stress, with variable effects on LDL cholesterol and triglycerides; one review concluded intermittent fasting is generally safe and did not increase disordered eating or disturb energy levels [7][10].

A review on women's health discusses intermittent energy restriction in women with overweight and with healthy weight, noting reduced adherence to daily restriction as a reason for developing intermittent regimens [6]. Reported dropout rates were 2 to 38 percent for intermittent fasting versus 0 to 50 percent for calorie restriction [1].

Because appearance goals usually depend on keeping muscle while losing fat, body composition is a focus of the research. Intermittent fasting typically reduces both fat mass and lean mass, and a 2025 narrative review proposes combining it with exercise to retain lean mass [4]. Wikipedia reports that alternate-day fasting does not appear to affect lean mass, although one review found a small decrease, and that most human studies report weight loss of 2.5 to 9.9 percent [1].

The 5:2 meta-analysis reported a reduction in fat-free mass alongside fat mass versus controls [8], and the 2024 network meta-analysis reported lean mass decline with short-term fasting [8]. A 2026 meta-analysis of 28 trials reported fat-free mass loss in both younger and older adults with low to very low certainty, and a scoping review of 20 trials in adults aged 45 and over reported generally small between-group differences in fat-free mass over mostly 12 weeks or less [8].

Short-term effects include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, which usually fade within a month [1]. It is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, older adults, underweight people, or those with or at risk of eating disorders [1]. Longer fasts are described as carrying risks such as refeeding syndrome and gallstones [11].

The US National Institute on Aging says research is limited and inconclusive and does not recommend these diets for the general public; the American Heart Association says there is no good evidence of heart-health benefits; the UK NHS advises people considering 5:2 to consult a physician first [1]. The American Diabetes Association noted limited evidence on safety in type 1 diabetes, and New Zealand's Ministry of Health (2017) said doctors may advise it for some people except those with diabetes [1].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums, fasting appears in cutting discussions as an alternative to daily calorie counting, usually through personal transformation posts such as the looksmax.org thread on 5/2 fasting, in which other members congratulated the poster [5].

A 2023 study reported that sustained alternate-day fasting potentiated doxorubicin cardiotoxicity in a trial and in mice, in work done in the context of fasting strategies being investigated in chemotherapy patients [18]. Wikipedia notes that intermittent fasting is not recommended to treat cancer in France, the UK or the US [1]. Wikipedia also reports that Ramadan fasting produced weight loss of up to 1.51 kg that was regained within about two weeks [1].
Related practices include time-restricted eating, whole-day water fasting, calorie counting and low-calorie formula diets, all of which target the same appearance outcome of reduced body fat [1][4].
